title: Small Folly, Big Consequences
overview: A collection of short sayings about how a little foolishness can undo a lot of good, especially in work, speech and the way rulers govern.

parts.label: A little folly spoils much (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Just as a few dead flies can ruin a jar of costly perfume, one foolish act can wreck a reputation built over years. The right hand was linked with skill and good judgment and the left with clumsiness, so the fool fumbles and shows what he is even on an ordinary walk.

parts.label: Staying calm before a ruler (v. 4)
parts.note: If someone in power is angry with you, do not storm off from your job or duty. A calm, gentle response can settle even serious offenses.

parts.label: The world turned upside down (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The writer has seen rulers give high posts to fools while capable, well-off people are passed over. Riding a horse was a sign of rank, so slaves riding while princes walk is a picture of a social order flipped by bad leadership.

parts.label: Everyday risks and skill (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Ordinary jobs like digging, knocking down walls, quarrying and chopping wood all carry hidden dangers, and a sharp blade does better than brute force. A snake charmer who acts too late earns nothing, which suggests that timing and good judgment matter; some readers also see a warning against stirring up trouble, though the exact point is debated.

parts.label: Fools and their words (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Wise speech wins goodwill, but a fool's talk starts silly, ends in harmful madness, and goes on and on about a future no one can actually know. Not knowing the way to town seems to be a saying for lacking even basic common sense.

parts.label: Good and bad leaders (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: A land suffers when its king is immature (the Hebrew word can mean a boy or a servant, so translations differ) and its officials feast from the morning on, while good leaders eat at a proper time to stay strong, and neglect brings a nation down like a sagging, leaky roof. Verse 19 may describe the careless attitude of such leaders, and the chapter closes by warning that even private insults against the powerful have a way of getting out, much like the saying "a little bird told me."

think: Have you seen one small lapse outweigh a lot of good in someone's life, and did that seem fair to you?
